title: Behind the Scenes at the Summer Fair: Movable Walls and Mending Motion
notice: Synthetic demo material. Invented document; no real meeting, publication, email or call occurred.

blocks.text: Welcome back to Emerald City Community Radio. I’m your host, and today we’re talking about the hands-on work that makes our festivals and parades come together. Joining me in the studio is Tamsin Reedwood, a stage carpenter with the Festival Committee. Tamsin, welcome.
Thank you. Glad to be here.
We’ve also got Oriel Brambleworth, a puppet maker from Green Market, joining us by wire. Oriel, can you hear us?
Yes, clearly. Thank you for having me.
Let’s start with you, Tamsin. I understand you’ve been solving a puzzle for the Summer Fair committee—how to make the pavilion work for different vendors from year to year.

That’s right. The old system was a mess of mismatched panels and borrowed flats. So I designed a set of wooden walls, all uniform. They’re on locking casters, so you can roll them into place, and they pin together with oak dowels. No nails, no fuss. We used them last summer to create three different booth layouts over the course of the fair. Afterward, we stacked them flat and stored them in the Festival Committee shed. They’ll be ready to go again this year.
And Oriel, your work is a bit more... animated. You were working on a piece for the Munchkin harvest parade?

Yes, a large wooden harvest spirit head. It’s a beloved piece, but its motion had gotten terribly jerky. The old metal hinge had rusted solid. Rather than replace it with another piece of metal that would just rust again, I carved a hardwood dowel to fit the pivot points exactly and used a supple leather strap to control the range of motion. It’s a more forgiving joint. Now the nod is smooth, almost serene. It should last for many more parades.
Tamsin, when you hear about Oriel’s solution—wood and leather instead of metal—does that resonate with how you think about materials?

Absolutely. You use what lasts and what you can repair. My walls are pine and oak—common, strong, easy to sand and re-seal if they get scuffed. Oriel’s fix is smarter than just swapping like for like. It understands the piece.

That’s kind of you to say. I think our work is similar in that way. We’re both asked to make something function, but the best solutions consider the life of the object. Your walls aren’t just for one day; they’re a system. My repair wasn’t just about making it move today, but ensuring it moves the same way years from now. There’s a rhythm to that kind of making.
It sounds like there’s a lot of forward thinking in what might seem like simple construction or repair. Oriel, did you have the materials on hand, or was it a special order?

The leather was from a strap I had. The wood was a scrap of applewood from a previous project—it’s dense and wears smoothly. Part of the craft is keeping a good inventory. You never know when a scrap will become the key piece.
Tamsin, what was the biggest challenge with the walls?

Getting the weight right. They had to be heavy enough not to tip if someone leaned on a booth, but light enough for two people to move. We hit the balance with a hollow-core design and the casters placed just so. Took a couple of prototypes to get it.

Well, the results clearly speak for themselves. Thank you both, Tamsin Reedwood and Oriel Brambleworth, for sharing a bit of the making behind our celebrations. Up next, the community calendar. You’re listening to Emerald City Community Radio.
